name: High-trust / low-trust face

card.summary: A looksmaxxing framework that says faces read as trustworthy or untrustworthy at a glance, so softening trust-related cues (eyes, brows, expression, skin, grooming) can improve how someone is perceived beyond bone structure alone.
card.aka: high trust face, low trust face, high trust, low trust
card.note: The forum framework is informal; the underlying face-perception research measures first impressions, not character.

quick.overview:
High-trust and low-trust are labels used on looksmax.org for how trustworthy, approachable and non-threatening a face looks on first sight. A high-trust face is described as warm and open; a low-trust face as cold, hostile or intimidating. Proponents argue that this impression can matter as much as, or more than, raw bone structure for how others respond to someone.

The idea parallels psychology research on first impressions, in which people rapidly judge trustworthiness and dominance from faces, and in which cues such as resting expression and brow and mouth shape shift those judgments. The research measures what viewers perceive; it does not show those perceptions are accurate.
quick.how: Community members post photos and ask whether their face reads high-trust or low-trust. Suggested adjustments discussed include relaxed or slightly upturned resting expression, eye and brow presentation, grooming, skin clarity and hairstyle, with threads on how to look more high-trust.
quick.risks: The framework is an informal community construct and the labels are subjective. Threads often treat the labels as fixed verdicts, which researchers on first impressions caution against, since face-based judgments are fast but weak predictors of actual character. Surgical or cosmetic changes pursued for this goal carry their ordinary risks.

lead: High-trust / low-trust face is a framework used in looksmaxxing communities, especially looksmax.org, for how trustworthy, warm and approachable a face appears at first glance. A high-trust face is described as friendly, open and non-threatening, while a low-trust face is described as cold, severe or menacing [2][12]. The framework is used to explain why two people with similar attractiveness ratings can receive different reactions from others.

For appearance, the idea points to features that are often adjustable: resting expression, brow position, the visible eye area, skin and grooming. Members post photos and ask for classification, and discuss how to look more high-trust [4][6][7]. Some threads argue the distinction is overstated or misapplied, and others ask whether it is a real phenomenon at all [5].

The terms echo academic work on first impressions. Psychologist Alexander Todorov and colleagues have studied how observers infer traits such as trustworthiness and dominance from faces within a fraction of a second, how two dimensions (valence and dominance) summarise those judgments, and how such inferences relate to outcomes such as election results [1][13]. The forum framework is informal and is not drawn directly from this literature, but the two share a core observation: faces carry an immediate impression of warmth or threat that observers report with confidence.

chain: Face cues (resting expression, brows, eyes, skin, grooming) shape the first impression
Viewers read the face as warmer or colder within a moment
Others respond with more or less openness
angle.text: Practitioners look at the cues that make a face read as warm or threatening and adjust the changeable ones: expression, grooming, hairstyle and skin. The aim is to be received as approachable rather than to change bone structure.

paras: In forum usage a high-trust face is one that looks gentle, kind or safe, often associated by posters with soft or upturned eye and mouth shape, relaxed brows, visible white of the eye and a neutral-to-pleasant resting expression. A low-trust face is one posters describe as hard, brooding or predatory, for example with a heavy brow, deep-set or hooded eyes, a narrow squint or a severe resting expression [2].

One widely shared thread contrasts the two types feature by feature, listing the eye area, jaw and chin and brows, and argues that the low-trust look reads as dominant while the high-trust look reads as likable [2]. Replies in the same thread show the usual range of the debate, with posters arguing over which look is preferable and which category given photos belong to [2].

Threads range from rating requests, such as asking whether specific eyes are low-trust or high-trust [6][7], to broader arguments that the quality decides how people are treated socially [8]. Several posters describe a personal shift between the two categories after changes in weight, grooming or expression [9]. Terms such as 'high trust normie' and 'high trust ogre' combine the trust label with the community's wider vocabulary for typical and unusually imposing-looking men [9][10].

The terms circulate in looksmax.org's face-analysis culture alongside concepts such as the blackpill, and appear in threads going back several years [10][11]. Looksmaxxing itself is described in encyclopedic sources as a self-improvement practice that grew out of incel and blackpill message boards in the 2010s and was later popularised by creators on TikTok and other platforms in the 2020s [12]. The framework is a community construct; no single originator is documented.

Posters have also written about how they came to adopt the idea, sometimes presenting a 'high trust pill' as a companion to the blackpill's emphasis on bone structure [11]. In this use, trust works as a second axis next to conventional ratings of symmetry, jaw and eye shape, which helps explain why the term is often paired with discussion of canthal tilt and eye-area traits that mainstream coverage of looksmaxxing has also described, such as the 'hunter eyes' trend [12].

Proponents say trust impressions form instantly, strongly affect social and dating treatment, and are partly independent of attractiveness. One thread titled around the claim that looking high-trust is everything states the strong version of this position [8]. Another argues that tall or imposing men are expected to signal harmlessness through constant smiling or joking in order to avoid being read as threatening [3].

Skeptics within the same community argue that the labels are used loosely, that it is hard to tell which features drive them, or that the explanation can be stretched to fit any outcome [5]. Posters also disagree about whether a low-trust look is a handicap or an asset, since some describe an intense, guarded look as a source of presence [2].

Members who want to read as warmer discuss changes that fall within ordinary grooming and self-presentation: a relaxed resting expression, softer brow position, hairstyle, skin clarity and facial hair, and weight or body-fat changes that alter the face's overall impression [4][9]. These are community suggestions rather than clinical advice, and the threads document before-and-after photos rather than controlled comparisons.
Some members also raise cosmetic or surgical options for the eye area. Those carry the ordinary risks of such procedures and are covered in the entries on the specific procedures.

Psychologists studying face perception find that observers form trait impressions such as trustworthiness from faces almost immediately and agree with one another to a notable degree [1]. Todorov's work, summarised in his 2017 book Face Value, argues that these impressions are consequential but are poor guides to actual character [1]. His Wikipedia biography lists studies of judgments made after a 100-millisecond exposure (Willis and Todorov, 2006), of how different photos of the same person produce different impressions (Todorov and Porter, 2014), and of how competence judgments from faces predicted election results (Todorov and colleagues, 2005) [1].

The best-known model of how people organise these judgments is the 2008 valence-dominance model by Oosterhof and Todorov. Participants rated 66 neutral-expression photographs on many traits, and a principal components analysis found two main dimensions: the first, interpreted as valence, explained about 63 percent of the variance, and the second, interpreted as dominance, about 18 percent [13]. Trustworthiness ratings tracked the first dimension and dominance ratings the second [13]. The 'trust' and 'threat' language of the forums maps loosely onto these two axes.

In follow-up experiments the authors generated 300 computer-made faces and exaggerated the trustworthiness dimension. At the negative extreme the faces were most often classified as angry, and at the positive extreme as happy, which led the authors to propose that trustworthiness judgments draw on features resembling emotional expressions [13]. The dominance dimension related more strongly to masculinity and maturity than to emotional expression [13]. This is relevant to the forum discussion of brows and mouth shape, because it suggests that features resembling a frown or smile at rest influence the impression.

A large multi-country replication reported that the two-dimension structure held broadly across world regions, with a possible third dimension in some regions [14]. Research also suggests that perceived health and personality judgments from faces are at least partly accurate, though the page summarising this work notes the evidence is varied [14]. Researchers describe trustworthiness impressions as a continuum measured by viewer ratings rather than as two categories [1][13]. No published trial has tested the forum's specific recommendations for looking more high-trust.

Mainstream coverage of looksmaxxing has focused on the movement's surgery, drug and mewing trends, its connection to incel forums, and critiques of its effect on young men, with outlets such as Vice, the BBC, Business Insider and The Conversation covering the wider scene between 2018 and 2024 [12]. The trust framework itself has received little separate coverage; it appears mainly in forum threads.
No studies found. Related academic work on social attributions from faces is described under Research and expert views [1][13].

timeline.event: Todorov and colleagues report that competence inferences from faces predict election outcomes [1].
Willis and Todorov publish a study of impressions formed after 100 milliseconds of exposure to a face [1].
Oosterhof and Todorov propose valence and dominance as the two dimensions of face evaluation [13].
Olivola and Todorov publish 'Elected in 100 milliseconds' on appearance-based inferences and voting [1].
Todorov and Porter show that different photos of the same person give different impressions [1].
Todorov publishes Face Value: The Irresistible Influence of First Impressions [1].
A multi-country replication examines the valence-dominance model across world regions [14].
Vice covers the 'hunter eyes' trend in looksmaxxing, one of the eye-area themes related to trust talk [12].
Threads asking 'how do i look more high trust' and 'is low trust high trust even a real thing' appear on looksmax.org [4][5].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, high-trust and low-trust are used both as descriptive tags and as claims about social outcomes [2][8]. Threads mix rating requests, advice and arguments about whether the category exists [5][6].

claims.claim: A face's trust impression matters as much as bone structure
claims.believers: Posters argue that being read as safe or threatening drives how people treat you and say it explains differences between similarly rated faces [8].
claims.experts: Research shows trait impressions from faces form quickly and affect some decisions, though they are weak predictors of real traits [1].

claims.claim: You can look more high-trust by changing expression, grooming and eye-area presentation
claims.believers: Members share tips and before/after photos in threads on how to look more high-trust [4].
claims.experts: Studies of face perception find expression-resembling cues shift trustworthiness ratings; no trial has tested the forum's specific recommendations [13].

claims.claim: High-trust vs low-trust is a real, useful distinction
claims.believers: Many posters sort faces into the two groups and treat it as obvious [2].
claims.experts: Academic researchers describe trustworthiness impressions as a continuum measured by viewer ratings rather than two categories [13]. Some forum members also question whether the idea is real [5].

claims.claim: Low-trust faces have a harder time socially unless they signal harmlessness
claims.believers: Posters say imposing men are expected to smile and joke to avoid being read as a threat [3].
claims.experts: Researchers report that negative-looking faces are judged as less trustworthy in ratings, while cautioning that such judgments do not reflect actual character [1][13].

claims.claim: Low-trust looks signal dominance and presence
claims.believers: The comparison thread says sharper, deep-set eyes give a dominant, intimidating gaze [2].
claims.experts: In the valence-dominance model, dominance is a separate dimension from trustworthiness and relates to masculinity and maturity cues [13].

claims.claim: A person can move from high-trust to low-trust (or back) through weight, grooming or expression changes
claims.believers: One poster describes no longer being read as a high-trust 'ogre' after changes [9].
claims.experts: Studies show different photos of the same person produce different impressions, so appearance in a given image changes ratings [1].

claims.claim: The 'high trust pill' is a necessary complement to the blackpill
claims.believers: Posters describe adopting trust as a second explanatory axis alongside structure [11].
claims.experts: Academic sources do not use the blackpill framework; face-perception research treats trait impressions as one factor among many in social outcomes [1].
